Additional sources of bias: Before-after design without a concurrent control, so secular trends and co-interventions cannot be excluded; the outcome is a population rate rather than paired per-patient measurements, so the per-sample potassium bias attributable to fist clenching is not quantified; fist clenching was identified by direct observation, not randomised
Notes: Primary outcome row. Direction of effect is ↑ because removing fist clenching lowered the rate of unexplained hyperkalaemia (16.0% -> 3.8%), i.e. fist clenching was raising potassium. The metric is a RATE of unexplained hyperkalaemia, not a measurement bias — so no absolute/percentage change in potassium and no APS comparison is possible. Across the 18 other specialist outpatient clinics, the rate fell from 5.4% (n=24,883) to 3.7% (n=34,169), a 32% fall (p<0.001) (p5).
